STATEMENT OF INTEREST 1
The Center for Reproductive Rights (the “Center”)
works to ensure reproductive rights are protected in law
as fundamental human rights. Since its founding in 1992,
the Center has litigated and appeared as amici before the
Supreme Court and state and federal courts in dozens of
cases about critical reproductive health and constitutional
issues, many of which raised standing to challenge laws
that impact contested healthcare access. The Center’s
litigation and policy also addresses issues around receipt
of information about healthcare, confidential access to
care, and the ability to autonomously consent, including
for young people. The Center submits this brief to support
core precedent that opens the federal courts only to
litigants who can demonstrate concrete, particularized,
and actual injury and causation when seeking to challenge
laws that may determine access to essential healthcare
and related information for others. This bedrock standing
principle has been a bulwark against litigants using the
federal courts to pursue moral, ethical, and consciencebased objections to laws that do not impose injury, in
accordance with the requirements of Article III, while
ensuring that the judicial process is available when people
face real harms around healthcare access.
SUMMARY OF ARGUMENT
Article III incontrovertibly requires a plaintiff to
establish an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized,
1. Pursuant to Supreme Court Rule 37.6, Amicus states that
no counsel for any party authored this brief in whole or in part, and
that no entity or person other than Amicus made any monetary
contribution toward the preparation and submission of this brief.

2
and demonstrably caused by the defendant. These
requirements are especially crucial when a challenger in a
lawsuit seeks to limit or restrict another person’s ability to
access healthcare, given that others’ health and well-being
is at stake. Petitioners here assert complex theories to
claim that Washington laws injure them by increasing the
likelihood of youth access to outpatient behavioral health
services, relying on speculation instead of real effects, and
factual misunderstandings about how the laws operate.
They follow an alarming trend by plaintiffs in recent cases
involving reproductive healthcare for others who have
jettisoned key limitations in asserting injury. In FDA v.
Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine , 602 U.S. 367 (2024),
this Court recently rejected the argument that standing
for unregulated plaintiffs can turn on a chain of thirdparty events with multiple contingent steps, noting that
these theories of harm invite a universe of speculation.
This case presents the same underlying problem, and
the Court should again reject standing that is based on
contingent facts that may never materialize.
Petitioners here misconstrue how the Washington state
laws operate in relation to healthcare access, asserting
harms that the laws do not by their terms impose. Resp.
Br. 6-12, 22. Factual confusion aside, their theories of
injury are unworkable in the healthcare context and would
allow for no meaningful limits on litigation by plaintiffs
with moral, ethical, or conscience objections to care.
Contrary to this Court’s precedent, Petitioners’ “object”
theory would enable those who oppose a healthcare law
to challenge any legal change that they claim impacts
their status, with no workable criteria for courts to apply.
Petitioners’ “increased-risk-of harm” theory would permit
challenges to any law or policy that supports access to

3
healthcare services that plaintiffs allege violate their
rights, based merely on a theoretical risk that it increases
the chances that access will occur. And Petitioners’
“voluntary changes to parenting strategies” theory would
condition standing on deeply felt but subjective reactions
to laws in the absence of direct regulation, resulting in a
deluge of litigation over reproductive healthcare policies
by both supporters and opponents of access. If accepted,
these boundless standing theories would enable challenges
to healthcare regulation across the country irrespective
of states’ different public policy approaches, including
to laws existing in a majority of states that mandate or
conversely limit parental involvement with reproductive
and sexual healthcare.
ARGUMENT
I. Plaintiffs’ Theories of Injury Upend this Court’s
Standing Doctrine, Including in Cases about
Healthcare Access.
Article III incontrovertibly requires a plaintiff to
establish an injury in fact that is concrete, particularized,
and demonstrably caused by the defendant. But plaintiffs in
recent cases involving sexual and reproductive healthcare
for others have jettisoned these key limitations in asserting
injury. In FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602
U.S. 367 (2024), this Court recently rejected plaintiffs’
attenuated assertions of injury and causation. Noting that
the plaintiffs’ arguments turned on a chain of third-party
events with multiple contingent steps, the Court refused
to expand Article III standing to accommodate plaintiffs’
theories. This case presents the same shortcomings, and
is not different because Petitioners assert injuries that

4
include infringement on parental rights. The Court should
once again reject assertions of standing that are based on
contingent facts and multiple layers of speculation that
may never materialize.
A. Article III’s injury-in-fact requirement is a
critical limitation in the healthcare context.
The “bedrock constitutional requirement” of Article
III standing requires a plaintiff to demonstrate they
have suffered or will suffer an injury in fact caused by
the defendant and redressable by a court order. All. for
Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 378 (quoting United States
v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670, 675 (2023)). To establish an injury
in fact, the plaintiff must identify the “invasion of a legally
protected interest” that is “concrete and particularized”
and “actual or imminent, not conjectural or hypothetical.”
Lujan v.Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555, 560 (1992) (citation
and internal quotation marks omitted). Time and again,
the Court has emphasized that neither the “‘intensity
of the litigant’s interest’” nor “strong opposition to the
government’s conduct” is a substitute for a concrete and
particularized injury. All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602
U.S. at 394 (quoting Valley Forge Christian Coll. v. Ams.
United for Separation of Church & State, Inc. , 454 U.S.
464, 486 (1982)); see also  Diamond v. Charles , 476 U.S.
54, 62 (1986) (“The presence of a disagreement, however
sharp and acrimonious it may be, is insufficient by itself
to meet Article III’s requirements.”). The Court has never
held that there is an alternative to showing concrete and
particularized harm, whether based on an attribute of
a statute, or the nature of the asserted rights violation.

5
An injury suffices for Article III standing only if
it is “fairly traceable to the challenged action of the
defendant, and not the result of the independent action
of some third party not before the court.” Lujan, 504
U.S. at 560 (citation, brackets, and ellipses omitted).
When, as here, the challenged conduct does not “require
or forbid some action by the plaintiff,” the plaintiff faces
the “‘substantially more difficult’” task of “linking their
asserted injuries to the government’s regulation (or lack
of regulation) of someone else.” All. for Hippocratic Med.,
602 U.S. at 368 (quoting Lujan, 504 U.S. at 562). In doing
so, this Court has explained, the plaintiff cannot rely
on “speculative links,” i.e., “where it is not sufficiently
predictable how third parties would react to government
action or cause downstream injury to plaintiffs.” Id. at
383. Nor can a plaintiff rely on “attenuated links,” i.e.,
“where the government action is so far removed from its
distant (even if predictable) ripple effects.” Id. The Court
has repeatedly admonished theories of standing that
rest on a “speculative chain of possibilities,”  Clapper v.
Amnesty Int’l USA , 568 U. S. 398, 410 (2013), especially
when those possibilities depend on “unfettered choices
made by independent actors,” Lujan, 504 U.S. at 562
(citation omitted).
Article III’s requirements that an injury be “concrete
and particularized,” Lujan, 504 U.S. at 560, and traceable
to the defendant, see Allen v. Wright , 468 U.S. 737, 738
(1984), are particularly crucial in suits against laws that
support healthcare access for people other than the
plaintiffs. That is because healthcare is distinct from many
circumstances raising standing for unregulated parties,
such as economic regulations that limit profits for thirdparty businesses, e.g., General Motors Corp. v. Tracy, 519

6
U.S.. 278, 287 (1997) (asserting standing based on harm
to financial interests of large purchaser of natural gas
that was liable for paying a tax imposed only on subset
of out-of-state sellers who were the regulated parties);
laws governing parks and national forests that impact the
people who use them, e.g., Summers v. Earth Island Inst.,
555 U.S. 488, 494 (2009) (asserting harm to recreational
interests of environmental organization’s members from
regulation applying to forest service decision process);
and property regulation that impacts the value of other
properties. See All. for Hippocratic Med ., 602 U.S. at
384-85 (discussing different types of cases where laws
may injure third parties for standing purposes).
Unlike business issues and those involving enjoyment
of natural resources and property, healthcare access
necessarily involves individuals who need treatment
directly impacting their bodies and sometimes the
sustenance of their lives. These individuals may lose
access to vital care and suffer devastating consequences
based on asserted harms to third parties. Given the
human stakes, it is imperative for an unregulated party
that wants to curtail healthcare for others to demonstrate
concrete injury, just as Article III requires.
B. This Court rejected “attenuated” or
“speculative” theories relying on third party
chains of action in Alliance.
Like Petitioners here, unregulated parties in recent
cases have tried to jettison the requirement that they
demonstrate a concrete, particularized, and actual or
impending harm when seeking to challenge laws that
neither require nor prohibit any action on their part, but

7
instead govern healthcare access for others. At bottom,
they allege what are disagreements with governmental
policy, or deeply-feared but hypothetical harms at the end
of a multistep chain of contingencies involving independent
actions by third parties. These standing theories lack
a principled endpoint and threaten to inundate the
courts with injured litigants, in defiance of this Court’s
precedents and Article III’s mandates.
This Court recently rejected that standing can turn
on a chain of third-party events with multiple contingent
or speculative steps in Alliance, the only case involving
an unregulated party’s challenge to healthcare access
for others it has recently decided. Just two years
ago, physicians who did not use or prescribe the drug
mifepristone asserted standing to challenge FDA’s actions
regarding the drug based on claims that if they had to
treat patients who experienced complications from the
medication, they might suffer future injuries to their
religious liberty rights or economic interests.
In rejecting the Alliance plaintiffs’ standing based
on both conscience injuries and economic injuries,
this Court focused on the “difficulty [of] establishing
causation” when the regulated party is not the plaintiff
and causation depends on the responses of regulated
parties “‘and perhaps on the response of others as well.’”
All. for Hippocratic Med.  602 U.S. at 383 (quoting
Lujan, 504 U.S. at 562). This Court held that a chain of
events that would require doctors to provide abortion
or related treatments in spite of federal laws that allow
conscience objectors to refuse was plaintiffs’ speculative
assertion. See id. at 383. Similarly, the Court rejected
a causal pathway that alleged economic harm from an

8
increase in patients with complications, the need to divert
resources to their treatment, and increased liability and
insurance costs. These things might never happen, the
Court explained, and federal regulation of mifepristone
would not have caused the doctors’ harms even if they did.
See id. at 386-90. Harm instead depended on actions by
third parties—patients, insurers, lawyers, others—each
of which was “highly speculative.”  Id. at 390. The Court
rejected the doctors’ “limitless” theory that would not only
allow physicians to challenge any FDA action approving a
new drug (virtually all of which come with complications
and risks) but also permit various kinds of plaintiffs to
challenge “almost any policy affecting public health” on
the basis that such actions may reach them through a
long chain of uncertain effects. Id. at 391-92. In requiring
direct and predictable personal harms, the Court held
that “a plaintiff ‘s desire to make a drug less available
for others does not establish standing to sue.” Id. at 374.
Although Alliance  dealt with physicians’ concern
about rights violations caused by patient access to
medication, and this case concerns parents’ concern
about rights violations if their children were to receive
a referral for behavioral healthcare, both cases involved
alleged constitutional injuries, and the requirement that
plaintiffs establish a concrete, particularized, and actual
or imminent injury, which remains “an essential and
unchanging part of the case-or-controversy requirement
of Article III,” All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602 U.S. at
380—not one that can be dispensed with depending on
the factual context.
Given the potent “value interests” involved on all sides
in reproductive and gender-related healthcare, All. for

9
Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 382 (citation omitted), it is
unsurprising that litigants assert harms to themselves
derived from potential access to services by others, and
fear consequential infringements on their own rights from
a chain of hypothetically possible events. For instance,
a federal district court recently held that physicians
and organizations with moral, ethical, and conscience
objections who did not provide abortion services lacked
standing to have Minnesota’s laws protecting abortion
access declared unconstitutional. Women’s Life Care
Center v. Ellison , 811 F . Supp. 3d 996 (D. Minn. 2025)
(appeal filed ). The laws did not impose any requirement
or prohibition on the plaintiffs, and the asserted injuries—
that Minnesota’s alleged under-regulation of providers
may lead more patients to show up at plaintiffs’ offices
with follow-on injuries—were the type deemed insufficient
for Article III in Alliance. And a Michigan federal court
recently rejected standing for a group of plaintiffs opposed
to abortion who sought to challenge the state’s newly
ratified constitutional amendment guaranteeing “the right
to make and effectuate decisions about all matters relating
to pregnancy, including but not limited to prenatal care,
childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, sterilization,
abortion care, miscarriage management, and infertility
care.” Right To Life of Mich. v. Whitmer , No. 25-1973,
2026 WL 1471210, at *1 (6th Cir. May 26, 2026) (quoting
Mich. Const. art. I, § 28(1)). The plaintiffs included a nonprofit that felt the amendment would limit its legislative
anti-abortion efforts, women who had been pregnant and
planned to be pregnant again who feared negative impacts
on their care, and parents of public school children who
alleged that the amendment would allow schools to aid in
activities that would violate their parental rights. Id. The
Sixth Circuit affirmed that the plaintiffs lacked standing

10
because they failed to show how the amendment or state
officials who were named defendants could cause their
asserted injuries. Id. at *2-3.
That the plaintiffs in these cases had deep and
subjectively real fears that laws addressing healthcare
would impact them through a chain of hypothetical events
is undisputed. But this Court has stated many times that
deeply-felt interests cannot stand in for concrete and
particularized personal harm. Valley Forge, 454 U.S. at
473 ; Allen, 468 U.S. at 756; United States v. SCRAP, 412
U.S. 669, 687 (1973). Maintaining this limitation is crucial
in the face of efforts to convert third-party actions and
access into legally cognizable injury that would quickly
extend to all forms of stigmatized care if the door were
opened, even in the absence of foundational Article III
requirements.
C. Attenuated theories of harm like those here
force courts to speculate about causation.
Unlike a basis for standing that relies on direct
enforcement of a law or regulation against a plaintiff,
theories of injury and causation in Alliance  required
multiple steps by third parties that vastly expand
speculative pathways for how plaintiffs will be impacted.
This case presents the same challenge, and the Court
should reject standing that is based on contingent facts
that may never materialize.
Here, Petitioners offer confoundingly “complicated
causation theories,” All. for Hippocratic Med.  602 U.S.
at 368, to connect the laws at issue to their assertions of
injury, articulated as a bucket of present harms around

11
changes to their current parenting, and a separate bucket
of potential future harms that turn on their children
running away to a licensed shelter and coming into contact
with the challenged laws. Pet’rs’. Br. 3-4, 18-19, 43, 50.
The causal chain leading from the challenged laws to
any of these asserted harms is inherently speculative,
requiring action by at least one and often multiple third
parties, including youth, shelters, youth department
authorities, and providers of behavioral health services.
Future harms turning on an inability to be involved with
their adolescent’s behavioral healthcare require a lengthy
string of theoretical events, including at minimum: youth
to run away to a shelter; to inform the shelter that they
are seeking gender-affirming care, and the shelter to
then notify the Department; youth to refrain from giving
contact information for parents; to accept a behavioral
health service referral; and to secure outpatient behavioral
health services without state assistance (which the law
does not provide for) before parents are contacted within
the statutorily required seventy-two hour period with
an offer of reconciliation services. See Resp. Br. 41-42.
For any alleged harm turning on longer-term outpatient
mental health treatment, the Department would need to
invoke a separate provision permitting an extended stay
in the shelter if parents do not request return of the youth
or cannot be reached. See Resp. Br. 6-7.
Stretching causation even farther, Petitioners’
asserted “present” harms to parenting depend on the
extra step of parents’  contemplation  of an attenuated
chain of events in which their children might run away
and trigger the law, involving even more speculation about
third-party actions and future contingencies, in addition

12
to parents’ subjective decisions to alter their behavior that
the law in no way requires. 2 See infra II.C.
Notably, showing the extent to which these chains
are speculative, the overwhelming majority of youth who
do run away stay with friends or family, not in licensed
shelters. National Center for Homeless Education,
Student Homelessness in America: School Years 2017-
18 to 2019-20  at 1 (2021), https://perma.cc/4CD8-NDRJ.
And, as Respondent’s brief explains, for youth who do go
to licensed shelters, the State offers them only contact
information for mental healthcare providers that is
readily obtainable online. Resp. Br. 23. “[I]t is irrational
to assume that children would run away from home to get
information they could easily obtain online.” Id. at 39-40.
Indeed, since the shelter laws were enacted more than
three years ago, licensed shelters have not once contacted
the Department about a runaway youth seeking genderaffirming care or reproductive care. Id. at 13.
2. Petitioners assert that these harms infringe on parental rights
and speech (a religious liberty claim appears to have been mooted
at this stage, Resp. Br. 22). While they focus mainly on parental
rights, to establish an injury in fact based on censored speech such
as their use of pronouns they would otherwise reject, it is similarly
not enough merely to rely on subjective fears. Laird v. Tatum , 408
U. S. 1, 11–16 (1972). This Court has held that a plaintiff cannot
establish an injury in fact by alleging only that their constitutional
speech rights are chilled “by the mere existence” of a government
program they perceive to be “inappropriate,” consider “inherently
dangerous,” or allegedly gives them a “generalized yet speculative
apprehensiveness” that the government “may at some future date”
take an action that “would cause direct harm.” Id.

13
On top of that, Petitioners’ fail to confront that the
shelters’ parental notification process cannot be the cause
of their asserted injuries because another law stands
in the way. Similar to the alleged conscience injuries
in Alliance , which the Court held were foreclosed by
conscience protections in federal law that broke the
causal chain, 602 U.S. at 390, Petitioners’ theories of
causation and redressability for the shelter law fail here.
This is because Wash. Rev. Code § 71.34.530, a different
statute dating to 1985, already allowed youth ages 13 and
older to request and receive outpatient behavioral health
treatment (but not medication or other physical treatment)
without parental involvement even prior to and in the
absence of the shelter law. Resp. Br. 14. Wash. Rev. Code
§ 71.34.530 confers this ability on youth whether they
are in a shelter or not, breaking the chain of causation
for the shelter law to cause Petitioner’s asserted injuries.
And while Petitioners also seek to challenge § 71.34.530,
they face no individualized harm that would give them
standing; that law is decades old, similar to many others
across the healthcare context, Resp. Br. 15, and does not
meet the criteria for Petitioners’ standing theories even
as they articulate them, as discussed in more detail below.
See infra II.A.
Even if not factually or legally foreclosed by the way
the laws operate, Petitioners’ harms depend on the kind
of speculation about the decisions of independent third
parties this Court has long recognized does not establish
injury in fact. See, e.g., All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S.
at 383; Clapper, 568 U.S. at 415. Petitioners must show that
“third parties will likely react in predictable ways that
in turn will likely injure them.” Clapper, 568 U.S. at 413
(internal citations omitted). And this Court has repeatedly

14
declined to endorse standing theories when key links in
the chain require it to engage in “guesswork as to how
independent decisionmakers will exercise their judgment.”
Id. Alliance reiterated these longstanding, key limitations
on federal judicial authority, even as plaintiffs try to loosen
them based on deeply-held but speculative fears around
sexual and reproductive healthcare as discussed above.
The Court should follow that established precedent here.
II. The Theories of Injury that Petitioners Assert
Would Open the Floodgates to Litigation Over
Healthcare Access.
Petitioners assert three theories of injury, each of
which is entirely unworkable in the healthcare context and
would place no meaningful limits on litigation by plaintiffs
who oppose access for others. First, Petitioners’ “object”
theory is unsupported by any case providing criteria
for courts to apply, and as articulated for the first time
here would enable plaintiffs to challenge any change to a
healthcare law that imposes or removes conditions under
which providers can offer a treatment to patients. Second,
Petitioners’ “increased-risk-of harm” theory would permit
challenges to any law or policy that supports access to
healthcare services that plaintiffs allege violate their
rights, based merely on a theoretical risk that it increases
the chances that access will occur. And third, Petitioners’
“voluntary changes to parenting strategies” theory would
condition standing on deeply felt but subjective reactions
to a law in the absence of direct regulation, resulting in a
deluge of litigation over reproductive healthcare policies
by both supporters and opponents of access. These
limitless standing theories would enable challenges to
healthcare regulation in every state, including when states

15
adopt a public policy requiring parental consent or notice
for youth access to sexual and reproductive services such
as abortion, prenatal care, and contraception; and when
they permit youth to confidentially and independently
obtain these types of care.
A. The “object of the law” theory is unworkable
in the healthcare context, and Alliance
functionally rejected it.
Seeking to sidestep the problems with attenuated
and speculative asserted injury in the absence of concrete
facts, Petitioners advance a sweeping theory that they
are “objects” of the law and have standing on that basis
alone, although they are not directly regulated, and even
absent a showing of individualized harm, causation, and
redressability. Petitioners rely on Diamond Alternative
Energy, LLC v. EPA , 606 U.S. 100 (2025) and Mirabelli
v. Bonta, 607 U.S. 492 (2026), cases that offered bare
gestures to an “object of the law” theory without detailing
what it would require, and certainly without holding that it
could obviate bedrock standing requirements. Plaintiffs in
these cases are dissimilarly situated to Petitioners, given
that they were already in direct reach of the laws they
challenged, without any need for attenuated and speculative
chains of events to inflict harm. 3 And Petitioners further
3. Neither Diamond  nor Mirabelli held that anyone whom the
government knows a law will affect or allegedly intends a law to
affect is an “object” of the law. Nor did they hold that anyone who is
indirectly implicated by a law is treated like a directedly regulated
party for the purpose of injury-in-fact. Diamond —in which injury
and causation were undisputed—did not involve a constitutional
right but rather the “‘familiar circumstance where government
regulation of one business may be likely to cause injuries” to other

16
ignore that Alliance functionally rejects such a theory, in
part because it would be unworkable in a healthcare access
context, like that Petitioners construe the Washington
laws to present.
Petitioners fail to offer coherent criteria to assess
when an unregulated party should be deemed the “object”
of a statute, reflecting that caselaw does not establish the
theory, and a decision accepting it here would drastically
distort precedent. They first suggest the “text and
design” of the shelter laws make “parents unwilling to
affirm their gender-confused children” the object of the
laws because they “reclassify parents” from “one legal
category to a less favorable one,” essentially “chang[ing]
. . . how the statute treats these parents.” Pet’rs’. Br 24-25.
This theory would make any unregulated person eligible
to challenge a change in healthcare law or policy if they
view its obligations as “less favorable” to them, or if it
authorizes providers to do something new or different to
which they object.
directly connected businesses based on “commonsense economic
principles.”606 U.S. at 116-17. In upholding standing, the Court
declined to resolve the question of whether fuel producers were in fact
objects of the regulations. Id. And Mirabelli—in holding that a class
of parents had standing to challenge policies adopted and employed
by schools that their children actually attended—included a single
unexplained reference to parents as “objects of the [law]”, see 607
U.S. at 498.  That aside, its central focus was on detailed allegations
by named plaintiffs that schools had already applied the challenged
law to their children. By contrast, Petitioners will come within the
reach of the challenged laws only after a series of intervening events,
including individualized decisions by young people, parents, shelters,
and outpatient behavioral healthcare providers.

17
For example, any change to a healthcare regulation
that imposes or removes conditions under which patients
can access a treatment—e.g. based on whether they
h a v e  h e al th  in s ur an c e ,  o r  h e al th  ris ks  an d  b e n e fi ts  f o r
groups with different attributes (including, for example,
pregnancy)—would automatically confer standing on
patients who oppose the changes to their status under
the law, irrespective of whether they would ever seek the
treatment, and even if they are not regulated parties.
The same goes for providers who would never provide a
type of healthcare and are not directly regulated, such as
when a regulatory scheme for a medication is altered in a
way that they believe is less favorable. But this reasoning
could have conferred standing on the plaintiff physicians
in Alliance based on numerous perceived negative changes
to their status and treatment under the law—for example,
through approval of nurse practitioners to prescribe the
medication along with physicians who previously had sole
privileges and the legal advantages that implies. All. for
Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. at 375-76. And while changes
to legal status could confer standing if a challenger showed
more specific likelihood of individual injury, causation, and
redressability—for example if a patient can show that they
use or are likely to use a treatment, or a provider offers
it—those changes must fail under an “object theory”
that is based simply on asserted legal “reclassification,”
particularly when the perceived change in category is
based solely on the regulation of others.
Second, Petitioners claim that statements made by
legislators before the bill’s passage show “a purpose to
thwart parental influence and authority” which makes
parents the “objects” of the law even though they are not
directly regulated. Pet’rs’. Br. 25. The cases that they

18
rely on for their glancing reference to “object” standing
make no mention of legislative history. See Diamond, 606
U.S. at 116 (looking to “commonsense economic realities”
to determine plaintiffs had satisfied redressability);
Mirabelli, 607 U.S. at 494 (involving parents who had been
denied information under the challenged policies or had
children in public schools that were following the policies).
Moreover, basing a standing theory on the purported
“stated purposes” of legislators is inherently subjective,
given that legislative bodies are diverse and statements
will conflict. See Resp. Br. 29 (“[F]loor statements by
individual legislators rank among the least illuminating
forms of legislative history” (quoting NLRB v. SW Gen.,
Inc., 580 U.S. 288, 307 (2017)).
A theory of standing based on an alleged purpose
to implicate groups that fall outside the regulation is
particularly unworkable in the healthcare context, where
laws operate through providers, medical institutions,
drug approvals, insurers, patients, and many other
interrelated entities, and legislative records are replete
with statements about complex purposes and effects.
Reflecting that complexity, this Court in Alliance rejected
physician plaintiffs’ standing to challenge regulation of a
medication that they would not prescribe or administer, in
spite of their assertions that calling on emergency doctors
to treat complications “is not a bug in the FDA’s abortiondrug plan, but part of its very design,” and the FDA had
repeatedly made statements showing that “the harm
caused [to emergency doctors like Respondents] is not just
predictable; it is embedded in FDA’s plan.” Resp. Br. in
Opp. 2, 25, All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. 367 (2024).
If, as Petitioners claim here, a mere “stated purpose” to
affect unregulated parties in allegedly rights-depriving

19
ways made them “objects” for standing without any actual
demonstrated involvement, cherry-picked statements
made in the course of healthcare regulatory processes
could enable the kind of challenge that Alliance rejected.
To the extent the “object” theory depends on either a
new legal disadvantage or intent to target an unregulated
group (which, as noted, this Court has never held), it
would certainly have conferred Article III standing on
the plaintiffs in Whole Woman’s Health v. Jackson , 595
U.S. 30 (2021). The Jackson  plaintiffs were abortion
providers bringing a constitutional challenge to Texas
statute S.B.8, which authorized private parties to file
civil actions in state court for injunctions and damages
against anyone they believed performed or assisted
in prohibited abortions, defined to include those that
at that time were protected and could not be banned
under Roe v. Wade . This Court held that the providers
lacked Article III standing to sue the state court clerks
and judges who would be responsible for docketing and
administering the private lawsuits, given that they were
not “adverse.” Id. The plaintiffs similarly lacked standing
to sue a private individual who opposed abortion and
was positioned to bring an S.B.8 lawsuit, but had so far
disclaimed an intent to do so, because they could not
show injury traceable to that individual’s conduct. Under
the ill-defined object theory that Petitioners assert here,
however, S.B.8 absolutely inflicted a devastating change
to providers’ legal status. And while S.B.8 intentionally
impeded standing by limiting who could enforce the
law, legislative intent to target and harm the rights of
providers to provide constitutionally-protected care was
the law’s raison d’etre. Whole Woman’s Health 595 U.S.
at 61 (Roberts, C. J., concurring in the judgment in part

20
and dissenting in part) (“The clear purpose and actual
effect of S. B. 8 has been to nullify this Court’s rulings.”).
If anything like an object theory of standing exists to
replace fundamental constitutional requirements of
imminent injury and causation, it would have conferred
standing on the plaintiffs in Jackson. But it does not, and
any application would cut against innumerable decisions
and core Article III requirements of this Court.
Further showing the “object” standing theory is not a
justiciable standard at all, Petitioners assert that parents
who object to “outpatient treatment” without parental
consent for their adolescents are also “objects” under a
separate state law that they challenge, Wash. Rev. Code
§71.34.530, which generally allows youth thirteen and
older to ask for and consent to outpatient mental health
treatment. Petitioners offer no argument or evidence
that this law, enacted in 1985, on its face negatively
“reclassif[ies]” parents or otherwise changes a parent’s
legal status as the amendments to the shelter law allegedly
do. Pet’r’s. Br. 24. Nor does anything about the law suggest
that its “stated purpose[ ]” is to undermine parental
authority. Pet’r’s. Br. 25. Petitioners’ object theory would
thus confer standing on anyone who subjectively asserts
negative impacts from a law that regulates others in the
healthcare system.
Apart from having children who are “capable of
understanding gender and running away,” Pet’rs’. Br. 29,
the single potential limitation that Petitioners obliquely
suggest is that only parents who object to their adolescents
consenting to outpatient behavioral healthcare may have
“object” standing, while other parents must rely on other
theories. Pet’rs’. Br. 30. Essentially, then, Petitioners

21
assert automatic standing to challenge a healthcare
regulation in the absence of other personalized and
specific harms for those who don’t like what they claim the
regulation does. Healthcare issues in which challengers
have voiced opposition to a policy and yet been found to
lack the necessary individualized harms for standing span
a range from vaccines, to reproductive health services,
to insurance coverage. See, e.g., Coal. for Mercury-Free
Drugs v. Sebelius , 671 F .3d 1275, 1276 (D.C. Cir. 2012)
(group whose members opposed the use of thimerosal in
vaccines lacked standing to challenge vaccine approval
given that members would refuse vaccines or could
obtain a thimerosal-free formula); All. for Hippocratic
Med., 602 U.S. at 386; Kinder v. Geithner , 695 F .3d 772,
776 (8th Cir. 2012) (plaintiff who objected to Affordable
Care Act individual mandate to obtain insurance beyond
“catastrophic” coverage lacked injury for standing
purposes because she was in fact eligible to purchase
a catastrophic plan and so would suffer no injury). A
standing rule that empowers unregulated parties to bring
suit, but only those who subjectively oppose the legislation,
would flood the courts with disputes untethered from the
very real harms that healthcare access regulation can
impose on those who directly experience its effects.
B. The “increased risk of future access to
healthcare” theory would inundate the courts
with injured litigants asserting hypothetical
harms.
Petitioners assert that “increased risk of harm”
from the mere enactment of the law—even prior to any
implementation—is an injury for standing purposes,
contesting the Ninth Circuit’s conclusion that increased

22
risk “does not replace the foundational rule that a future
injury must be imminent in order to satisfy the injuryin-fact requirement.” Pet’rs’. Br. 50. This theory would
permit challenges to any law or policy that supports access
to healthcare services that plaintiffs allege violate their
rights, based merely on a theoretical risk that it increases
the chances that access will occur.
Petitioners variously suggest basing this “increased
risk” standard on “probability” of injury, id. 48, or
“predictable effect,” id. 52, or increased probability
“compared to the risk before the laws’ enforcement
began,” id. But they offer no discernable limits on when
any of these metrics would apply. The absence of limits
reflects that any law supporting access to healthcare
services—at least in theory—increases the risk of access,
creates a theoretical “predictable effect” that third parties
will access services, and raises the probability of access
as compared to before the law’s passage. To take one
example, regulatory approval for a method of contraception
increases the theoretical risk that a pharmacist with
conscience objections will need to prescribe it. A public
insurance coverage requirement for contraception on its
face creates a “predictable effect” that patients will seek
to fill more prescriptions that “may be likely” to conflict
with pharmacists’ objections. If allegedly objectionable
forms of contraception were not approved, the risk of these
harms would theoretically decrease. Indeed, an “increased
risk of harm” theory would likely confer standing on the
providers in Alliance, where the Court noted that FDA’s
approval and regulation of mifepristone may predictably
“yield more visits to doctors” because “virtually all drugs
come with complications, risks, and side effects.” All.
for Hippocratic Med. , 602 U.S. at 392. But it held that

23
speculative and attenuated intervening chains of events
defeated Article III requirements.
Importantly, as in Alliance, Petitioner’s theory is not
limited to increased risk of a future rights violation based
on a law’s application to their own actions, but instead
turns on third-party youth seeking care. A standing
theory based on increased risk of future harm that is
triggered by access to healthcare by others—whether
patients, beneficiaries, or youth—would make vital forms
of care vulnerable to challenge from the moment a law
is enacted, even without facts showing that a challenger
faces individualized harm. Even more problematic, the
more available and relied-on a form of healthcare is, the
higher the risk of it being used, bolstering standing for
anyone who objects and claims a related violation of their
rights, however hypothetical.
C. The “voluntary changes to parenting strategies”
theory would give parents sweeping leeway to
challenge a policy based on their subjective
reactions.
Even while asserting future harms or increased risk
of harm, no Petitioner has alleged their own behavior or
their children’s behavior has brought them within reach
of the statutes. Resp. Br. 12 (citations omitted). Still,
Petitioners claim that they have made voluntary presentday decisions to change their approach to parenting—
from using different pronouns, to not disciplining their
children—because of their undisputed opposition to
gender-affirming treatment. But this kind of speculative
and subjective reaction to a law cannot confer standing,
however deeply felt. See All. for Hippocratic Med. , 602

24
U.S. at 368 (“Article III standing screens out plaintiffs
who might have only a general legal, moral, ideological,
or policy objection to a particular government action.”).
Article III’s limitations on injuries of this kind are
essential to prevent a deluge of litigation over reproductive
healthcare policies, likely initiated by both supporters
and opponents of access in states that have enacted laws
limiting or facilitating care.
That parents may change their behavior in response
to reproductive health law and policy is a truism. For
example, a parent who objects to abortion in a state that
lifts an abortion ban may limit their child’s activities that
they believe increase the risk of pregnancy—from dating
to unsupervised time with friends—out of fear that the
child could become pregnant and choose termination
under state law provisions. That same parent could choose
an opposite parental strategy, concealing their opposition
to abortion from their child in the hopes of being consulted
about decisions they make. On the other side of the issue, a
parent who supports reproductive autonomy in a state with
an abortion ban may push their child to use a long-acting
form of contraception, such as an intrauterine device
(IUD), because they fear the consequences of unexpected
pregnancy without a range of choices available. Certainly,
parents across the country have made similar choices in
response to different legal regimes. Arleigh Rogers &
Michael Goldberg, Families with Transgender Kids Are
Increasingly Forced to Travel Out of State for the Care
They Need , AssOcIAted press  (July 10, 2023) , https://
perma.cc/4D4X-6NE8.
Regarding parental involvement specifically, legal
regimes in states across the country vary widely, based on

25
different public policy approaches. For example, 37 states
mandate parental involvement in a young person’s decision
to have an abortion, with varying requirements, while the
remainder allow a young person to independently and
confidentially seek care. Guttmacher Institute, Minors’
Access to Abortion Care (Aug. 1, 2026), https://perma.
cc/7FT9-TC3X. Conversely, 38 states and the District of
Columbia have enacted laws that permit youth to consent
to prenatal care; and 49 states and the District of Columbia
have laws that allow youth to consent to STI testing and
treatment. Abigail English & Rebecca Gudeman, Minor
Consent and Confidentiality A Compendium of State and
Federal Laws, Nat’l Ctr. for Youth L. (Aug. 2026), https://
perma.cc/E38X-HH3Y. While some parents believe lack
of opportunity for notice and consent injures their rights,
others perceive injury from state-mandated involvement
with personal decision-making of their children. Parents
with these different beliefs and views may voluntarily
adapt their parenting based on what laws allow or require.
If such adaptations become the basis for legal standing,
any such law—or state failure to require involvement—
will be open to challenge by parents regardless of whether
it is likely to directly impact them or their children.
But precedent makes clear that contingent choices
about parenting cannot satisfy Article III. This Court has
repeatedly rejected the idea that plaintiffs can create their
own injury, in particular when their responses could go
one way or another, or are “riddled with contingencies and
speculation that impede judicial review.” Trump v. New
York, 592 U.S. 125, 131 (2020). Alliance’s core teaching was
to reject a chain of causation that is not “predictable.” And
how a parent will voluntarily change behaviors in response
to health access regulation is inherently speculative.

26
So too here. Any causal chain from the challenged
laws to Petitioners’ assertion of present interference with
parenting runs through the unpredictable black box of
parents’ personal decision-making—as it should. Parents
can properly decide how to talk to, instruct, and discipline
their children in diverse ways, but that does not confer
standing to challenge a law that does not regulate them,
based on how they carry out their objections to it. Any
such rule would enable endless litigation irrespective of
how states choose to require or limit parental involvement
with healthcare access for youth, based on deeply-held
convictions that must inform parenting, but cannot be a
basis for challenging laws in the absence of the concrete,
particularized, and actual injury that Article III has
always required.

27
CONCLUSION
The judgment of the court of appeals should be
affirmed.
